o: Explain how authentication and account lockout reduce unauthorised access.
Explain how encryption protects intercepted data.
Describe the purpose of authorised penetration testing.
c: Long, unique passwords make guessing harder. Multi-factor or two-step authentication adds a separate proof of identity.
Limiting repeated incorrect login attempts reduces opportunities for brute-force guessing.
Encryption converts readable plaintext into ciphertext using an algorithm and key. Captured data is not readily understandable without the correct key.
An authorised test looks for weaknesses so they can be fixed before attackers exploit them. It must be carried out with explicit permission and an agreed scope.

m.title: Protect a school account
m.q: A school wants to reduce the chance of attackers signing in with guessed passwords. Explain how strong passwords and account lockout help. [4 marks]
st: The risk is many attempted password guesses.
Long unique passwords increase the number of possibilities [1], making guessing the correct password harder [1].
A lockout policy blocks further attempts after repeated failures [1], reducing how many guesses an attacker can try [1].
Two protections, each explained with how the attacker is limited.

w: A staff member accesses sensitive files away from school. Explain why two-factor authentication is useful. [4 marks]
The login needs an additional independent authentication factor [1], such as a code on a separate device [1]. A stolen password alone is therefore insufficient [1], reducing unauthorised access [1].
A website sends account information across the Internet. Explain why encryption is important. [4 marks]

The data is transformed from readable plaintext [1] into scrambled ciphertext [1]. If transmission is intercepted [1], attackers without the appropriate key cannot readily read the original information [1].
A college hires authorised testers before launching an online system. Explain the purpose and two benefits of penetration testing. [4 marks]

Authorised testers examine the system for vulnerabilities [1], using a defined scope [1]. They report weaknesses [1], allowing the organisation to correct them before malicious attackers exploit them [1].
wSteps: Identify the second proof needed beyond a password.
An additional factor and an example [2].
A stolen password alone is insufficient and access is harder [2].
The login needs an additional independent authentication factor [1], such as a code on a separate device [1]. A stolen password alone is therefore insufficient [1], reducing unauthorised access [1].
Trace readable data into scrambled data.
Intercepted ciphertext cannot be read normally without the key [2].

The data is transformed from readable plaintext [1] into scrambled ciphertext [1]. If transmission is intercepted [1], attackers without the appropriate key cannot readily read the original information [1].
Distinguish authorised testing from an unauthorised intrusion.
Testing is permitted and designed to find weaknesses [2].
Reporting allows fixes before real attacks [2].

Authorised testers examine the system for vulnerabilities [1], using a defined scope [1]. They report weaknesses [1], allowing the organisation to correct them before malicious attackers exploit them [1].

k.q: Safely simulate an account lockout decision using a supplied count of failed attempts.
k.code:
failed = 4
if failed > 3 then
    print("Account locked")
else
    print("Login still available")
endif
p: Print "Contact IT if needed" after the IF.
k.a:
With 4: Account locked. With 2: Login still available.

Extended OCR ERL:
failed = 2
if failed > 3 then
    print("Account locked")
else
    print("Login still available")
endif
print("Contact IT if needed")

Only a safe educational simulation; it does not authenticate users.

Explain how strong passwords, encryption and penetration testing improve network security. [6 marks]

Source: Original J277-style question; not an OCR past-paper original.

Strong passwords are difficult to guess [1], reducing unauthorised logins [1]. Encryption scrambles transmitted data [1], protecting contents if intercepted [1]. Authorised penetration testing identifies vulnerabilities [1], enabling patches/improvements [1].
v: Checking that someone is who they claim to be.
Using two different forms of evidence to sign in.
Temporarily blocking access after repeated failed attempts.
Transforming readable information into unreadable ciphertext.
x: Penetration testing should be conducted only with permission from the system owner.
r: Monitors/filters network traffic [1] according to rules to block unauthorised traffic [1].
Attempts many possible passwords [1] to discover the correct one/gain access [1].
Deceptive messages impersonate a trusted source [1] to trick users into revealing personal data/credentials [1].
Two devices follow the same web communication protocol. Explain two benefits. [4 marks]
Shared rules mean request/response formats are understood [1] so they can exchange data [1]. Common standards enable compatibility across makers [1], avoiding bespoke protocols for each device [1].
